title: A Vesta Range Hood Just Scored 9.7 out of 10. Here Is What the Reviewers Found
excerpt: We usually let other people do the talking, and this time someone said it better than we ever could. The review team at House and Beyond tested a Vesta under ca
body: We usually let other people do the talking, and this time someone said it better than we ever could. The review team at House and Beyond tested a Vesta under cabinet range hood and gave it 9.7 out of 10, calling it one of the best under cabinet range hoods for the money. For a brand that has been building kitchen appliances in Canada since 2010, that score sums up the whole idea. Serious performance without the showroom markup.

So what earns a score like that? Reviewers tend to judge a range hood on the same things home cooks care about. Does it actually pull smoke out of the kitchen? Is it quiet enough to hold a conversation? Does it look like it belongs in the room? And does it keep working after the first year? The Vesta scored well across all four.

Power comes first. Vesta under cabinet models move serious air for their size, with baffle filters that catch grease instead of letting it coat your cabinets. Baffle filters matter more than most people realize. They handle high heat better than mesh, they do not clog as fast, and they go straight into the dishwasher when they need cleaning.

Quiet is the second test, and it is where cheap hoods fail. A fan you refuse to turn on is a fan that does nothing. Vesta pairs efficient motors with thoughtful airflow design, so the hood can run at a level you will actually use every day, not just when the smoke alarm is already complaining.

Then there is the design. Reviewers at BrandChoose have placed Vesta alongside names like KitchenAid, GE, and Broan, pointing to the seamless construction and the heat sensor that adjusts suction on its own. There are no sharp seams to trap grease, and the lines stay clean in both modern and traditional kitchens.

For New York, this matters in a specific way. Apartment kitchens are small, cooking is often intense, and venting is rarely perfect. A hood that is strong, quiet, and easy to clean is not a luxury in that setting. It is the difference between cooking at home and ordering in.

Mercer & Co. New York brings the full Vesta line to dealers and homeowners across the New York area, including under cabinet, wall mount, island, and insert models up to 1000 CFM. If you are choosing a hood for a renovation, start with our guide to calculating the right CFM, then compare under cabinet and wall mount styles in The Mercer Journal.
A 9.7 is not our number. It belongs to the reviewers. But it is exactly the standard we are happy to be judged by.

title: Custom Range Hood Covers Are Trending. The Insert Inside Is What Matters
excerpt: Scroll through any kitchen renovation feed right now and you will see the same project again and again. Homeowners are building custom covers around their range
body: Scroll through any kitchen renovation feed right now and you will see the same project again and again. Homeowners are building custom covers around their range hoods, finished in plaster, microcement, wood, or painted drywall, and the results look like they cost a fortune. One creator said the cover saved her family about twenty thousand dollars compared with a contractor quote. The trend is real, and the finished look is hard to argue with.

Here is the part the videos rarely explain. A custom cover is only a shell. It captures nothing. The machine doing the actual work is the range hood insert hidden inside the box, and if that insert is weak, undersized, or loud, the prettiest cover in the world will not save your kitchen from smoke and grease.

So if you are planning a custom cover, choose the insert first and build the cover around it. Start with size. The insert should cover the full width of your cooktop, and the cover should be built a little wider than the insert so cooking fumes have room to collect before the fan pulls them in. A 30 inch cooktop usually pairs with a 30 or 36 inch insert.

Next is power. Match the CFM to how you cook. Light cooking with a lot of steaming and simmering can work with 600 CFM. Frequent stir frying, searing, and wok cooking needs 750 CFM or more, because high heat pushes a fast rising plume of smoke that a weak fan simply misses. Our guide to calculating the right CFM walks through the math room by room.

Ducting decides the rest. If your home allows it, vent the insert outside through the shortest, straightest duct run you can manage. Every sharp turn steals airflow. If outside venting is impossible, a ductless setup with charcoal filters is the fallback, and our ducted versus ductless guide explains how to decide for a New York apartment.

A few features are worth paying for inside the box. Baffle filters trap grease better than mesh and go straight into the dishwasher. A DC motor runs quieter, which matters when the kitchen opens into the living room. Bright LED lighting helps more than people expect, because the cover casts a shadow right where you are trying to cook.

Vesta makes inserts built for exactly this kind of project, including the Montreal insert in 24, 30, and 36 inch sizes and the Vancouver insert for 30 and 36 inch covers. Both are stainless steel, use dishwasher safe baffle filters, and are designed to disappear inside a custom cover while doing the heavy lifting.

The takeaway is simple. Let the cover be the fashion. Let the insert be the machine. Choose the machine first, size the cover to fit it, and your trending kitchen project will cook as good as it looks.
Related reading: How to Calculate the Right CFM for Your Range Hood, and Ducted vs Ductless: How to Decide for a NYC Apartment, both in The Mercer Journal.

title: How to Calculate the Right CFM for Your Range Hood
excerpt: CFM (cubic feet per minute) tells you how much air your range hood moves. Too little and smoke lingers; too much and you are paying for power you do not need.
body: CFM (cubic feet per minute) tells you how much air your range hood moves. Too little and smoke lingers; too much and you are paying for power you do not need.
The simple rule: for a gas cooktop, you need 100 CFM for every 10,000 BTU. A standard 4-burner gas range puts out about 40,000 BTU, so 400 CFM is your starting point.
For electric cooktops, the math is easier: 100 CFM for every 10 inches of cooktop width. A 30 inch cooktop needs about 300 CFM.
New York kitchens are often compact with lower ceilings, so most home cooks land in the 400 to 600 CFM range. Professional-style ranges with a grill or wok burner can push you toward 800 or more.
One more check: if your duct run is long or has several turns, add 100 CFM to compensate for the airflow loss. When in doubt, going slightly bigger is safer than going too small.
Related reading: Under Cabinet vs Wall Mount: How to Choose on The Mercer Journal.

title: Under Cabinet vs Wall Mount: How to Choose
excerpt: The choice between an under cabinet and a wall mount range hood comes down to one question: where is your cooktop?
body: The choice between an under cabinet and a wall mount range hood comes down to one question: where is your cooktop?

If your cooktop sits under existing kitchen cabinets, an under cabinet hood tucks neatly underneath. It saves space and keeps the clean line of your cabinetry. This is the most common setup in New York apartments.
If your cooktop is on a wall with no cabinets above it, a wall mount (chimney style) hood is the answer. It mounts directly to the wall and the chimney covers the ductwork up to the ceiling.
For kitchens with a cooktop on an island, you would look at an island hood instead, which hangs from the ceiling.
Measure your space first: the hood should be at least as wide as your cooktop, and mounted 24 to 30 inches above it for the best capture.
Related reading: How to Measure for a 30 or 36 Inch Range Hood on The Mercer Journal.

title: How to Measure for a 30 or 36 Inch Range Hood
excerpt: Range hoods come in standard widths to match your cooktop: 30 inches for a standard range, 36 inches for a wider pro-style range.
body: Range hoods come in standard widths to match your cooktop: 30 inches for a standard range, 36 inches for a wider pro-style range.
Step one: measure the width of your cooktop, not your counter. Your hood should match this width or be slightly wider. Never go narrower than the cooktop.
Step two: measure the mounting height. For most homes, the bottom of the hood should sit 24 to 30 inches above the cooking surface. Gas ranges do better at the higher end of that range.
Step three: check your ceiling height and cabinet depth. Under cabinet hoods need at least 12 inches of cabinet depth above them, and the duct needs a clear path out.
If you are between sizes, size up. A 36 inch hood over a 30 inch range captures more smoke at the edges, which is where most hoods lose performance.
Related reading: Ducted vs Ductless: How to Decide for a NYC Apartment on The Mercer Journal.

title: How to Clean Baffle Filters (They Are Dishwasher Safe)
excerpt: Baffle filters are the curved metal panels inside your range hood that trap grease. Unlike mesh filters, they are built to last and easy to clean.
body: Baffle filters are the curved metal panels inside your range hood that trap grease. Unlike mesh filters, they are built to last and easy to clean.
For weekly upkeep, just run them through the dishwasher. The hot water and detergent cut through grease without any scrubbing. That is the whole routine for most home cooks.
For a deeper clean every few months, soak the filters in a sink of hot water with dish soap and a quarter cup of baking soda for 15 minutes, then rinse.
Never use steel wool or harsh oven cleaner on baffle filters. It scratches the finish and shortens their life.
Clean filters are not just about looks. A clogged filter chokes airflow, makes the fan louder, and forces the motor to work harder. Ten minutes in the dishwasher keeps your hood running like new.
Related reading: How to Calculate the Right CFM for Your Range Hood on The Mercer Journal.

title: Ducted vs Ductless: How to Decide for a NYC Apartment
excerpt: A ducted range hood vents cooking air outside your home. A ductless (recirculating) hood filters the air and blows it back into the kitchen. In New York apartme
body: A ducted range hood vents cooking air outside your home. A ductless (recirculating) hood filters the air and blows it back into the kitchen. In New York apartments, this choice is often made for you.
Many NYC buildings, especially co-ops and rentals, do not allow new ductwork through exterior walls. If you cannot cut a vent to the outside, ductless is your option.
Ductless hoods use charcoal filters to trap odors and grease. They work well for everyday cooking, but the charcoal filters need replacing every 3 to 6 months depending on how much you cook.
If your building does allow ducting, ducted is the stronger choice. It removes heat and moisture completely instead of recirculating it, and there are no filters to replace.
Either way, match the hood to your cooking. Heavy wok or frying cooking benefits most from ducted venting; lighter everyday cooking does fine with a good ductless setup.
Related reading: How to Clean Baffle Filters (They Are Dishwasher Safe) on The Mercer Journal.
